size.note: Newman's Birds gives 43 cm. Wikipedia gives 44–47 cm.

habitat: Lakes, lagoons, marshes, sewage ponds and streams, solitary.
summary: A small buff heron. Outside breeding the upperparts are paler and less contrasting, the bill is yellowish with a blackish culmen, and the legs are normally pale yellow. The legs are pinkish red for a few days when breeding. In flight it looks like a white egret unless the biscuit-coloured or pale orange upperparts show. Young birds are darker above and have broader neck streaks.

similar.note: Cattle Egret is larger, walks with grazers, and is white except for summer buff plumes. Squacco Heron looks white only in flight; at rest the upperparts are buff or pale orange.

population.notes: Kemp et al. 2001 order-of-magnitude threshold 2^6=64 mature individuals (visiting breeder); paper interval half–double → 32–128.

sources.title: Kemp A.C., Herholdt J.J., Whyte I. & Harrison J. (2001). Birds of the two largest national parks in South Africa: a method to generate estimates of population size for all species and assess their conservation ecology. S. Afr. J. Sci. 97: 393–403.

bill.shape: yellowish with a blackish culmen outside breeding

head.pattern: Non-breeding upperparts are paler and less contrasting. Legs are pinkish red for only a few days when breeding.

wings.pattern: In flight the bird looks white unless the biscuit or pale orange upperparts are visible.

viewNotes.note: Buff or pale orange at rest, with a yellowish bill and pale yellow legs.
Streaked crown and a pale face. Young birds have broader neck streaks.
Biscuit or pale orange upperparts. The white of the wings is mostly a flight mark.
Looks white from above unless the pale orange back shows.
Looks like a white egret from below.

calls.description: Newman does not describe the voice. The texts do not separate the sexes. The catalogue cut is not labelled by sex. Grade A, recorded in Kruger.

research.note: Status is resident and all twelve months are listed. Newman calls it a common to very common resident. Wikipedia describes the European population as a migrant that winters in Africa, so Kruger may also receive those birds. The few days of pink breeding legs were not stored as a summer plumage. Chick down is not described. The call is grade A from Kruger.
